notes.bp: ASR should work across languages, accents, and dialects rather than only on well-resourced standard varieties.
notes.wh: A single average benchmark can hide failures on communities that have little representation in training or evaluation.
notes.naive: Report one multilingual score on a narrow, convenient test set.
notes.ap: Build a broad public test suite and an online evaluation process that makes language-variety performance visible.
notes.mech: ML-SUPERB 2.0 evaluates models on 200+ languages, accents, and dialects through DynaBench and compares five challenge submissions with baselines.
notes.math: Language-identification accuracy and character error rate are reported separately for general, accented, and dialectal speech.
notes.ww: The best submission reports 23% absolute LID improvement and 18% CER reduction generally, with 30.2% lower CER and 15.7% higher LID accuracy on accented/dialectal data.
notes.limits: Challenge submissions, test-suite composition, and hidden evaluation define the boundary; the results do not prove equal service quality for every language variety.
notes.title: The ML-SUPERB 2.0 Challenge: Towards Inclusive ASR Benchmarking for All Language Varieties

notes.bp: Child ASR needs a correction stage that fixes transcription errors without turning child-specific disfluencies into fluent but wrong text.
notes.wh: Child speech has unusual acoustics and language patterns, and child error-correction data are scarce.
notes.naive: Apply adult speech error correction directly to child hypotheses.
notes.ap: Create a large hypothesis-to-reference dataset for children and learn a generative correction model whose errors can be inspected by type.
notes.mech: CHSER contains 200K pairs across ages and speaking styles; fine-tuned generative correction is tested in zero-shot and ASR-fine-tuned settings.
notes.math: Word error rate measures overall correction, while substitution, deletion, insertion, and disfluency analysis show which errors are changed.
notes.ww: The paper reports up to 28.5% relative WER reduction zero-shot and 13.3% after ASR fine-tuning, but insertions and child disfluencies remain difficult.
notes.limits: The corpus, languages, ASR hypotheses, and correction model bound the result; preserving clinically meaningful disfluencies outside these settings remains open.
notes.title: CHSER: A Dataset and Case Study on Generative Speech Error Correction for Child ASR

notes.bp: An ASR system should recognize speech played through a loudspeaker, not only clean speech recorded directly by a microphone.
notes.wh: Loudspeaker playback changes the acoustic path and can add coloration, reverberation, and level differences that the recognizer may mistake for speech variation.
notes.naive: Train and test on direct recordings, then assume the model will transfer to playback speech.
notes.ap: Measure the distribution shift caused by loudspeaker emission and evaluate recognition under that realistic channel.
notes.mech: The paper studies ASR performance for loudspeaker-emitted speech and compares recognition across the tested playback conditions.
notes.math: Word error rate exposes the channel penalty; the useful distinction is speech content versus the acoustic path that carries it.
notes.ww: The paper reports a measurable ASR impact from loudspeaker emission under its experimental conditions.
notes.limits: The result is bounded to the loudspeaker, room, microphones, and ASR systems tested; other devices and adaptive compensation remain open.
notes.title: Effect of Loudspeaker Emitted Speech on ASR performance

notes.bp: Researchers need vowel measurements from child field recordings without manually transcribing and aligning every sample.
notes.wh: Child speech, dialect, recording conditions, and imperfect boundaries make automatic alignment unreliable.
notes.naive: Trust an automatic transcript and forced alignment without checking its acoustic measurements.
notes.ap: Use a semi-automatic pipeline, manually correct transcripts, and adapt the alignment model toward the child dialect.
notes.mech: WhisperX transcription and MFA alignment are evaluated on 275 Scottish-English children; acoustic vowel measures are compared with manual annotation.
notes.math: Agreement of vowel measures with manual data is the target; transcript correction and acoustic-model adaptation are separate interventions.
notes.ww: Manual correction improves measures, adaptation helps, and more training data does not automatically add improvement.
notes.limits: The result is tied to Scottish English, field recordings, and vowel measurements; other ages, dialects, and measures need separate validation.
notes.title: A semi-automatic pipeline for transcribing and segmenting child speech

notes.bp: Clinical speech studies need acoustic features that mean the same thing when extracted by different tools.
notes.wh: OpenSMILE, Praat, and Librosa can implement nominally similar features differently, changing a model's clinical conclusion.
notes.naive: Use one toolkit and treat its feature names as interchangeable with another toolkit's names.
notes.ap: Standardize extraction settings, compare tools directly, and test whether disagreements change group classification.
notes.mech: Three toolkits are applied to 77 schizophrenia-spectrum and 87 control speakers; correlations and classification performance are compared.
notes.math: Feature correlations, agreement for F0/formants, and AUC reveal whether a feature is reproducible and useful for discrimination.
notes.ww: F0 percentile agreement is high, but F0 variation and formants can disagree or even correlate negatively; F0 mean, HNR, and MFCC1 exceed AUC .70 in the reported classification.
notes.limits: The clinical groups, recordings, parameter choices, and tool versions define the boundary; no clinical diagnosis or deployment safety follows from these correlations.
notes.title: Comparative Evaluation of Acoustic Feature Extraction Tools for Clinical Speech Analysis

notes.bp: A conversational agent should build rapport by responding proactively, personally, and with small listener signals rather than waiting for explicit requests.
notes.wh: Naturalness depends on timing and interaction, so a response strategy can affect both dialogue flow and a person's willingness to share.
notes.naive: Optimize a language model for task content while ignoring backchannels and stalls.
notes.ap: Prompt an LLM with a coordinated strategy for proactive behavior, personalization, and aizuchi backchannels, then measure both conversation and participant outcomes.
notes.mech: CO-STAR and few-shot prompts drive a robot in human-robot interaction; stalls, dialogue similarity, robot backchannels, participant behavior, and questionnaires are evaluated.
notes.math: The paper separates system behavior from participant behavior and subjective reports rather than treating one dialogue score as rapport.
notes.ww: The integrated strategy is reported to improve behavioral and subjective rapport measures.
notes.limits: The study is bounded to the robot, prompts, participants, and short interaction protocol; long-term trust, cultural variation, and causal attribution remain open.
notes.title: Rapport-Building Dialogue Strategies for Deeper Connection: Integrating Proactive Behavior, Personalization, and Aizuchi Backchannels

notes.bp: Speech restoration should use clues about the recording environment to undo distortion without mistaking the environment for speech content.
notes.wh: The same linguistic content can be damaged differently by noise, reverberation, or other conditions.
notes.naive: Condition a generator only on linguistic or speaker representations.
notes.ap: Add an acoustic-context representation that describes the distortion and its intensity, then condition the restoration model on it.
notes.mech: ACX refines CLAP-derived environmental embeddings and conditions the diffusion restoration model UNIVERSE++ across distortion conditions.
notes.math: Restoration quality and stability across conditions compare context-aware and content-based conditioning; variability itself is an evaluation target.
notes.ww: The paper reports better restoration and reduced performance variability with acoustic context.
notes.limits: The result is tied to the distortion set, CLAP features, and diffusion backbone; unseen devices, rooms, and perceptual listeners remain open.
notes.title: Listen through the Sound: Generative Speech Restoration Leveraging Acoustic Context Representation

notes.bp: A virtual agent should move in ways that fit what it is saying without requiring a hand-written rule for every situation.
notes.wh: Rules do not generalize, while purely data-driven gesture generation is costly and often tied to one embodiment.
notes.naive: Choose gestures from fixed rules or train a large motion generator for each agent.
notes.ap: Use an LLM to plan context and select reusable primitive actions that can be adapted across agents.
notes.mech: The proposed model uses LLM-driven primitive action selection for co-speech motion in virtual agents and robots.
notes.math: The key object is the mapping from dialogue context to a sequence of primitive actions; the paper's abstract does not expose a complete quantitative comparison.
notes.ww: The paper presents a flexible and scalable approach, but the preserved evidence does not establish a numerical gain.
notes.limits: Full mechanism, baselines, human judgments, and cross-embodiment transfer require the paper's detailed evaluation; the result is not a claim of human-like motion.
notes.title: Co-Speech Motion for Virtual Agents in Dialogue Using LLM-Driven Primitive Action Selection

notes.bp: Speech features used in behavioral or clinical models should measure the intended behavior consistently across people and contexts.
notes.wh: Open-source tools can disagree, and those disagreements can change model performance unevenly across demographic groups.
notes.naive: Extract features from a familiar toolkit and assume the outputs are reliable.
notes.ap: Compare tools directly in the target population and test how feature differences alter models and group behavior.
notes.mech: OpenSMILE and Praat features are evaluated on adolescents with autism from audio-visual recordings, with model performance compared across contexts and demographics.
notes.math: Feature agreement and downstream classification are both measured; this connects measurement reliability to fairness rather than stopping at correlation.
notes.ww: The paper reports considerable tool variation that influences model performance across context and demographic groups.
notes.limits: The population, features, tools, and behavioral tasks define the boundary; the study does not identify one universally correct toolkit.
notes.title: Can We Trust Machine Learning? The Reliability of Features from Open-Source Speech Analysis Tools for Speech Modeling

notes.bp: ASR should adapt to a new or low-resource domain when labels are scarce or noisy.
notes.wh: Pseudo-label errors can reinforce themselves, while self-supervised adaptation alone may not learn the task boundary.
notes.naive: Fine-tune only on the small labeled target set or apply one adaptation technique in isolation.
notes.ap: Cascade self-supervised representation adaptation with pseudo-label training so each stage prepares the next.
notes.mech: MSDA evaluates a two-stage Meta PL pipeline for Greek and weakly supervised ASR, with ablations of the cascade.
notes.math: Recognition error and ablations test whether the order of self-supervision and self-training matters.
notes.ww: The paper reports state-of-the-art results and finds the cascading combination necessary in its experiments.
notes.limits: The languages, pseudo-label quality, source models, and domain shifts bound the claim; robustness to severely wrong pseudo-labels remains open.
notes.title: MSDA: Combining Pseudo-labeling and Self-Supervision for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in ASR

notes.bp: An audio captioner should describe what happened naturally and accurately, not exploit a similarity score with repeated or awkward words.
notes.wh: CLAP rewards can favor semantically related phrases while ignoring repetition and human naturalness.
notes.naive: Optimize one embedding similarity metric directly.
notes.ap: Combine CLAP similarity with repetition penalties, clipping, and LLM feedback during reward optimization.
notes.mech: CRRP trains an automated audio-captioning system with a stabilized CLAP reward and an LLM evaluator; semantic, human, and AI assessments are compared.
notes.math: The reward combines semantic alignment and language naturalness, while multiple evaluations expose metric-specific behavior.
notes.ww: The paper reports strong semantic and human/AI evaluation results for the proposed reward system.
notes.limits: The result depends on caption datasets, evaluator prompts, and reward weighting; human agreement and out-of-domain audio remain open.
notes.title: Optimizing CLAP Reward with LLM Feedback for Semantically Aligned and Diverse Automated Audio Captioning

notes.bp: A dialect identifier should distinguish all Arabic varieties without requiring the data and model size of a full-resource system.
notes.wh: Dialects share language identity while differing in sound and vocabulary, and country coverage is uneven.
notes.naive: Train on a few prominent dialects or assume a large model automatically solves data imbalance.
notes.ap: Release broad data and compare pretrained encoders, data-size reduction, and model capacity directly.
notes.mech: ADI-20 contains 3,556 hours across 19 dialects plus MSA; ECAPA-TDNN and Whisper encoder systems are evaluated.
notes.math: F1 measures dialect identification while controlled reductions test the value of data volume and parameters.
notes.ww: Using 30% of the original data causes only a small F1 decrease in the reported experiments.
notes.limits: The country/dialect inventory, labels, and data collection define the boundary; conversational code-switching and unrepresented varieties remain open.
notes.title: ADI-20: Arabic Dialect Identification dataset and models

notes.bp: Spoken-language understanding must fit a constrained device without losing intent and slot decisions.
notes.wh: Distillation can preserve a teacher's behavior that later quantization cannot represent.
notes.naive: Compress by distillation and quantize afterward as unrelated steps.
notes.ap: Train the student with distillation and quantization constraints together through multiple stages.
notes.mech: QUADS jointly optimizes a pretrained SLU model for low-bit regimes and evaluates it on SLURP and FSC.
notes.math: Accuracy measures task retention, while GMACs and model size measure compute and storage cost.
notes.ww: The paper reports 71.13% SLURP and 99.20% FSC accuracy, 60–73x lower GMACs, and 83–700x smaller models with bounded degradation.
notes.limits: The result depends on tasks, bit settings, and hardware interpretation of the counts; latency and energy on deployed devices remain open.
notes.title: QUADS: Quantized Distillation Framework for Efficient Speech Language Understanding

notes.bp: A deepfake dataset for public figures should resemble the speech impersonation attacks people actually encounter, not merely contain clean synthetic clips.
notes.wh: Collection, segmentation, synthesis method, and speaker identity all affect how realistic a fake sounds.
notes.naive: Collect convenient speech and generate one kind of synthetic audio without checking human confusion.
notes.ap: Build a documented pipeline for high-quality bona-fide data, transcription-based segmentation, and several synthesis regimes, then measure naturalness and confusion.
notes.mech: The paper creates bona-fide and synthetic speech for ten public figures and reports NISQA-TTS and human misclassification.
notes.math: Dataset composition, automated naturalness, and human confusion measure different parts of realism.
notes.ww: The dataset reports NISQA-TTS naturalness 3.69 and a highest human misclassification rate of 61.9%.
notes.limits: The ten figures, synthesis systems, listeners, and dataset protocol bound the result; new generators and adversarially chosen public speech remain open.
notes.title: Collecting, Curating, and Annotating Good Quality Speech deepfake dataset for Famous Figures: Process and Challenges

notes.bp: A hearing test for adolescents with cochlear implants should measure vocal-emotion perception in an interface they can tolerate and engage with.
notes.wh: Pseudospeech removes linguistic emotion clues, while interface burden can affect participation and test time.
notes.naive: Use a computer-only test and treat usability as separate from measurement validity.
notes.ap: Compare a robot and computer interface on the same emotion task, including sensitivity, duration, and participant preference.
notes.mech: Adolescents aged 10–17 complete EmoHI pseudospeech emotion tests with a computer and NAO robot; d-prime, duration, and usability are measured.
notes.math: Sensitivity, test duration, and perceived usability/enjoyment expose the tradeoff between measurement equivalence and engagement.
notes.ww: Sensitivity is similar (.36 versus .37); the robot takes longer, is less usable, but is more enjoyable and engaging.
notes.limits: The participants, robot, pseudospeech task, and small sample bound the result; long-term adherence and general hearing-device populations remain open.
notes.title: Robot-assisted Recognition of Vocal Emotions in Pseudospeech for Cochlear Implanted Adolescents

notes.bp: An augmentative communication system should let a minimally verbal child express personal concepts and a personally meaningful voice.
notes.wh: Fixed symbols and fixed voices limit relevance, identity, and the range of things a user can communicate.
notes.naive: Offer a static symbol board and one default synthetic voice.
notes.ap: Generate visual symbols and use zero-shot TTS so users can personalize both the concept representation and voice.
notes.mech: The proposed AAC system combines text-to-image generation with zero-shot TTS for children with autism.
notes.math: The conceptual objects are symbol coverage, voice personalization, and eventual social validity; the paper's abstract does not report a completed comparative trial.
notes.ww: The paper presents a broader expressive design but leaves long-term communication outcomes for future study.
notes.limits: No causal benefit or clinical efficacy should be inferred; user satisfaction, safety, cultural fit, and long-term adaptation remain open.
notes.title: From Static to Dynamic: Enhancing AAC with Generative Imagery and Zero-Shot TTS

notes.bp: A diarization system should assign speech to the right people in meetings with many simultaneous speakers without a separate pipeline for every case.
notes.wh: Overlap and speaker-count variation make it hard to learn all mixture configurations, while modular systems accumulate errors.
notes.naive: Train on a few-speaker simulation or chain independent detection and clustering modules.
notes.ap: Use one end-to-end non-autoregressive model and scale pretraining across systematically represented eight-speaker mixtures.
notes.mech: EEND-TA is evaluated on AliMeeting, AMI, DIHARD III, and MagicData RAMC with speed and diarization error comparisons.
notes.math: Diarization error rate measures missed, false, and wrongly attributed speech; multiple corpora test transfer across meeting conditions.
notes.ww: The paper reports 14.49% DER on DIHARD III and state-of-the-art results on the listed datasets.
notes.limits: The simulations, corpora, speaker counts, and model speed define the boundary; spontaneous conditions beyond these meetings remain open.
notes.title: Pushing the Limits of End-to-End Diarization

notes.bp: Researchers need to see many dimensions of voice data together rather than inspect one acoustic measure at a time.
notes.wh: High-dimensional features are difficult to extract, subset, and interpret without a usable exploratory interface.
notes.naive: Export one feature table and rely on fixed plots or isolated measures.
notes.ap: Put feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, filtering, and projection into an interactive dashboard.
notes.mech: Voxplorer exposes precomputed high-dimensional voice data and can extract features from recordings directly for interactive exploration.
notes.math: The object is an exploratory mapping from many acoustic dimensions to a visual projection; it is a research instrument rather than a predictive model.
notes.ww: The paper presents a reusable dashboard intended to broaden voice-analysis exploration; no scientific performance score is claimed.
notes.limits: Usability, projection choices, and feature-tool assumptions determine what researchers see; the dashboard does not establish causal voice categories.
notes.title: Voxplorer: Voice data exploration and projection in an interactive dashboard

notes.bp: An articulatory synthesizer should model not only sound traveling through the vocal tract but also sound radiating through its walls.
notes.wh: A simple physical model must reproduce speaker-specific radiation without adding an impractical number of parameters.
notes.naive: Ignore wall radiation or use one fixed radiation response for every speaker.
notes.ap: Represent each tract section as a damped spring-mass system and fit wall parameters to real speaker voicebars.
notes.mech: The simulated radiation from tube sections is compared with six speakers producing /b,d,g/ in vowel contexts, with parameters optimized to real spectra.
notes.math: Frequency-domain root-mean-square error between simulated and natural voicebar spectra measures how well the physical model explains the radiation.
notes.ww: The paper reports 2.26–3.82 dB RMSE from 0–800 Hz and concludes the simple model can reproduce the spectra closely.
notes.limits: The six speakers, selected consonants/vowels, frequency range, and fitted parameters bound the claim; other speech sounds and independent physical validation remain open.
notes.title: Evaluation of a model for sound radiation from the vocal tract wall

notes.bp: A listener may want one sound from a spatial mixture, and the system should use both where it is and what it is.
notes.wh: Nearby sources can overlap spatially, so direction alone may not distinguish the target.
notes.naive: Apply a spatial beamformer using only a target direction.
notes.ap: Condition an ambisonic-to-ambisonic separator on direction plus semantic information about the target sound.
notes.mech: SoundSculpt is trained on synthetic and real ambisonic mixtures, with direction from pointing and semantic embeddings from visual/audio description.
notes.math: Separation quality compares spatial-only and spatial-plus-semantic conditioning, especially for nearby secondary sources.
notes.ww: The paper reports that semantic conditioning helps when sources are spatially close and outperforms signal-processing baselines.
notes.limits: Synthetic/real mixtures, semantic encoders, and target descriptions define the boundary; spoken conversation and pointing errors remain open.
notes.title: SoundSculpt: Direction and Semantics Driven Ambisonic Target Sound Extraction

notes.bp: Children learning a second tonal variety must realize pitch targets while their physiology and first dialect continue to shape production.
notes.wh: Targets overlap in time and similar tones can interfere, so an error is not simply a failure to memorize a contour.
notes.naive: Treat each tone as an isolated fixed pitch template.
notes.ap: Analyze on-target and off-target realization as interacting targets shaped by physiology and dialect experience.
notes.mech: Pitch production from 139 Changli-exposed children aged 35–71 months is analyzed in the CL-CHILD corpus.
notes.math: The comparison separates target approximation, physiological constraints, and mutual interference among tonal categories.
notes.ww: The paper reports universal physiological constraints, persistent dialect interference, and off-target forms arising from phonetic similarity and target interaction.
notes.limits: The age range, dialect exposure, corpus, and tone inventory bound the developmental claim; longitudinal and other language environments remain open.
notes.title: Pitch Target Realization in Putonghua Tone Production of Children from Dialect-Speaking Regions

notes.bp: A neural vocoder should produce detailed speech quickly without adding aliasing, blur, or other audible artifacts.
notes.wh: GAN vocoders can be sharp and fast but their frequency behavior can create artifacts that aggregate quality scores miss.
notes.naive: Use a generic GAN vocoder and rely on its learned filters to suppress artifacts.
notes.ap: Add a learnable frequency-domain artifact filter that imposes explicit control over which spectral components pass.
notes.mech: AF-Vocoder inserts GAFilter into a GAN vocoder and tests reconstruction quality and artifact suppression across datasets and speakers.
notes.math: The frequency filter is the intervention; reconstruction and artifact measures compare quality in-domain and for out-of-domain speakers.
notes.ww: The paper reports better reconstruction quality and artifact suppression than other GAN vocoders.
notes.limits: Datasets, speaker coverage, artifacts, and listening protocol define the claim; real-time hardware cost and unseen languages remain open.
notes.title: AF-Vocoder: Artifact-Free Neural Vocoder with Global Artifact Filter

notes.bp: Researchers need emotional speech from people with Parkinson's disease to study how disease and emotion interact in voice.
notes.wh: Small clinical datasets make it hard to separate emotional variation from speaker, disease, and language variation.
notes.naive: Reuse a generic emotion corpus or collect labels without documenting participant and recording choices.
notes.ap: Create a dedicated New Zealand English database with multiple emotions, speakers, and acoustic analysis, then test human recognition.
notes.mech: EMOPARKNZ contains 1,950 recordings from 13 speakers across five emotions; acoustic measures and a 22-listener perception test are reported.
notes.math: F0, intensity, rate, and five-way listener accuracy connect measurable speech changes to perceived emotion.
notes.ww: The paper reports emotion-dependent acoustic differences and 63% listener classification accuracy.
notes.limits: Thirteen speakers, New Zealand English, Parkinson's disease, and the selected emotions bound the resource; clinical severity and broader populations remain open.
notes.title: Introducing EMOPARKNZ: the Emotional Speech Database from New Zealand English Speakers with Parkinson’s Disease

notes.bp: A voice-conversion system should change emotional expression for a speaker it has never seen while preserving the words and identity.
notes.wh: Emotion and identity are entangled, and changing one can distort the other; unseen speakers remove the shortcut of memorized target voices.
notes.naive: Train a separate converter for each target speaker or treat all speech variation as one undifferentiated style code.
notes.ap: Use diffusion with disentangled content, speaker, and emotion mechanisms plus expressive guidance for zero-shot conversion.
notes.mech: The model is trained on a large emotional-speech corpus and evaluated on unseen speakers in in-domain and out-of-domain data.
notes.math: Emotion accuracy, naturalness, and speech quality are separate targets; zero-shot splits test whether the conversion survives a new speaker.
notes.ww: The paper reports expressive converted speech with high emotional accuracy, naturalness, and quality on its reported tests.
notes.limits: The result is bounded to the training corpus, emotion set, diffusion design, and unseen-speaker protocol; identity verification, languages, and independent listening remain open.
notes.title: ZSDEVC: Zero-Shot Diffusion-based Emotional Voice Conversion with Disentangled Mechanism
